details:
**"Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird"**
Stevens's poem of thirteen short, haiku-like sections, each giving a different view of a blackbird. It opens "Among twenty snowy mountains, / The only moving thing / Was the eye of the blackbird," and ends "It was evening all afternoon. / It was snowing." It is one of the most frequent giveaways for Stevens.

**"O thin men of Haddam, / Why do you imagine golden birds?"**
A famous section of "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," which scolds the people of Haddam, Connecticut, for imagining exotic golden birds instead of seeing the ordinary blackbird. Other sections contrast "the beauty of inflections" with "the beauty of innuendoes," describe icicles filling a window "with barbaric glass," speak of knowing "noble accents / And lucid, inescapable rhythms," and describe a man who rides over Connecticut "in a glass coach" and is frightened by "the shadow of his equipage."

**"The Emperor of Ice-Cream"**
A short poem set at a wake for a dead woman. It opens "Call the roller of big cigars, / The muscular one, and bid him whip / In kitchen cups concupiscent curds," and tells the boys to "bring flowers in last month's newspapers." Its refrain is "The only emperor is the emperor of ice-cream."

**"Let be be finale of seem"**
A line from "The Emperor of Ice-Cream." It asks that appearances give way to reality, in keeping with the poem's acceptance of death and of the pleasures of the present.

**The dresser of deal and the "horny feet"**
The second stanza of "The Emperor of Ice-Cream" asks someone to take a sheet from a cheap pine ("deal") dresser that lacks "the three glass knobs," the sheet on which the dead woman "embroidered fantails once." The sheet is spread to cover her face, but if her "horny feet protrude," that shows "how cold she is, and dumb."

**"Sunday Morning"**
A meditative poem in which a woman stays home from church, enjoying "complacencies of the peignoir, and late / Coffee and oranges in a sunny chair." She thinks about "silent Palestine, / Dominion of the blood and sepulchre," and wonders whether earthly beauty is enough without heaven. It asks "What is divinity if it can come / Only in silent shadows and in dreams?" and answers that "Divinity must live within herself." It ends with "casual flocks of pigeons" that "sink, / Downward to darkness, on extended wings." Harriet Monroe first published a shortened version of it in Poetry magazine.

**"Death is the mother of beauty"**
The repeated central claim of "Sunday Morning," which holds that mortality is what gives earthly things their value. The poem also imagines a "ring of men" who chant "in orgy on a summer morn" to the sun, "not as a god, but as a god might be." Helen Vendler's study of Stevens's longer poems, On Extended Wings, takes its title from the poem's last line.

**Harmonium**
Stevens's first collection (1923). It contains "Thirteen Ways of Looking at a Blackbird," "The Emperor of Ice-Cream," "Sunday Morning," "Anecdote of the Jar," "The Snow Man," "Le Monocle de Mon Oncle," "Disillusionment of Ten O'Clock," "Peter Quince at the Clavier," "Domination of Black," and "The Comedian as the Letter C."

**"Anecdote of the Jar"**
A poem in which the speaker places a jar "in Tennessee, / And round it was, upon a hill." The jar makes "the slovenly wilderness" surround that hill. The jar, "gray and bare" and "tall and of a port in air," takes "dominion everywhere" and "did not give of bird or bush, / Like nothing else in Tennessee."

**"The Idea of Order at Key West"**
A poem about a woman singing by the shore who "sang beyond the genius of the sea" and becomes "the single artificer of the world / In which she sang." The speaker asks his companion, the critic Ramon Fernandez, why the lights of the boats in the harbor seemed to arrange the night after she stopped singing. It shows Stevens's idea that the imagination imposes order on reality.

**"The Snow Man"**
A one-sentence poem saying that "one must have a mind of winter" to regard frosted, snow-covered trees without hearing "misery in the sound of the wind." It ends with the listener who, "nothing himself, beholds / Nothing that is not there and the nothing that is."

**"Disillusionment of Ten O'Clock"**
A poem complaining that the houses are "haunted / By white night-gowns," not green or purple ones "with yellow rings." None of the sleepers will "dream of baboons and periwinkles." Only an old, drunken sailor "catches tigers / In red weather."

**"The Comedian as the Letter C"**
Stevens's long poem about Crispin, a poet who sails from Bordeaux to the Yucatan and then to Carolina, abandoning his romantic ideals for local reality. It opens by calling man "the intelligence of his soil" and "the Socrates of snails," and its section "The Idea of a Colony" imagines a colony of poets.

**"The Man with the Blue Guitar" and Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction**
In "The Man with the Blue Guitar," listeners complain that the guitarist "does not play things as they are," and he replies that "things as they are / Are changed upon the blue guitar." He also says "I cannot bring a world quite round, / Although I patch it as I can." Notes Toward a Supreme Fiction is Stevens's long poem setting out his idea of poetry as a "supreme fiction." In "A High-Toned Old Christian Woman," he writes that "Poetry is the supreme fiction, madame."
